ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A block wall $100$ feet long and $7$ feet high will be constructed using blocks that are $1$ foot high and either $2$ feet long or $1$ foot long (no blocks may be cut). The vertical joins in the blocks must be staggered as shown, and the wall must be even on the ends. What is the smallest number of blocks needed to build this wall?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows two layers of rectangular blocks; the vertically adjacent vertical joints above and below are not aligned; the vertical joints of one layer fall at the middle positions of the blocks in the other layer, indicating that adjacent horizontal layers must be arranged staggered. The illustration also reflects that this staggering can be understood as the joints of one layer being at even positions, and the joints of the adjacent layer being at odd positions. Reasoning: The wall is 100 feet long and 7 feet high; each block is 1 foot high, so there are 7 horizontal layers in total. Each layer can only use blocks of length 1 foot or 2 feet. If a certain layer adopts joints at positions 2,4,6,...,98, then the whole layer can be composed of 50 blocks of length 2 feet, requiring 50 blocks. Adjacent layers must be staggered, with joints at positions 1,3,5,...,99; in order for the two ends of the wall to be flush, this kind of layer must start with a 1-foot block and end with a 1-foot block, with 49 2-foot blocks in between, so it requires 2+49=51 blocks. The 7 layers must alternate between these two layer types. To make the total number of blocks minimal, let the more economical 50-block layer appear 4 times, and the 51-block layer appear 3 times. The total is 4×50+3×51=200+153=353.

The vertical joins in the blocks must be staggered as shown, and the wall must be even on the ends. What is the smallest number of blocks needed to build this wall?

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as showing the required stagger: one horizontal course can have vertical joints at positions 2, 4, 6, ... from the left end, while the adjacent course is shifted so its joints occur at positions 1, 3, 5, ... . From the text, the wall is 100 ft long and 7 courses high, with each course made of 1-ft-high blocks of length 1 or 2. Count blocks per course: an unshifted 100-ft course can use fifty 2-ft blocks, so it has 50 blocks. A shifted course with joints at odd positions must start and end with 1-ft blocks, with forty-nine 2-ft blocks between them, so it has 51 blocks. Since adjacent rows must alternate these two course types and the wall has 7 rows, choose the cheaper pattern for 4 rows and the more expensive pattern for 3 rows. Total = 4·50 + 3·51 = 353.

method.method_draft: Begin from the area/maximum-length-block lower bound.
